title: York man was held at gunpoint over incorrect Flock hit. Sheriff blames illegal tag cover

reading.body:
This is a false positive in an automated license plate reader, and the failure happened at the handoff between the alert and the enforcement action. A machine-generated match was treated as sufficient grounds to stop a motorist at gunpoint, so an error produced by the system became a use of force against a person the system had misidentified. The misread was a single character, and nothing between the camera and the deputy appears to have caught it.

Catching it would have required verifying the alert before acting on it. The vendor itself says such alerts should be independently verified before enforcement, which places the check at the point where the match was converted into a stop. A human comparison of the plate or the vehicle against the stolen-vehicle record would have been the step that broke the chain.

What is not established is why the reader misread the plate. The sheriff's office attributed it to an illegal tinted plate cover, and that is the department's account rather than an independent finding. The same office described the deputy's actions as reasonable, which is its own assessment and not a ruling by anyone outside it.

reports.title: York man was held at gunpoint over incorrect Flock hit. Sheriff blames illegal tag cover

summary: Steven Melvin, a 42-year-old motorist in York County, South Carolina, was held at gunpoint for more than five minutes after a Flock Safety license-plate reader misread the first letter of his plate and matched his BMW to a similar stolen vehicle. The sheriff’s office later said an illegal tinted plate cover caused the error and called the deputy’s actions reasonable. Flock said such alerts should be independently verified before enforcement.
